# Italus - The Lightening Tree
## Book 1, Chapter 1

The ground told him first.

Luca noticed it on a morning in late autumn when he was thirteen, moving the sheep past the north ridge where the old pines stood. The earth under his heel had changed. Not visibly—the scattered needles lay as they always did, amber and brittle on the limestone—but the pressure of the ground answered differently. Where he had stepped a hundred times along this shepherd's trail, a finger-width of fresh soil had risen, then settled again, like flesh that had been pressed and was still remembering the shape of the touch.

He knelt and placed his palm flat against it.

The soil was cool but not cold, and beneath the coolness ran a faint vibration, so subtle it might have been his own pulse reflected back. He pulled his hand away and looked toward the tree itself.

The pine stood perhaps forty paces up the slope. It was old enough that calling it a tree felt inadequate—it was more the architecture of one, a massive trunk that had begun its slow spiral upward perhaps two centuries before Luca was born, its needles still dense and dark green along the upper crown but sparse along the lower limbs, which meant either great age or recent strain. The tree had always been there. It was the kind of landmark shepherds used to locate themselves—the Leaning Pine, though Luca had never understood why it was called that. All pines leaned something, bent by the perpetual wind that moved through the Pollino Heights.

But this one was not where it had been.

He stood and walked toward it, his gaze moving from the base of the trunk to the ground around it. The limestone was scored fresh, pale where the weathering had not yet darkened it. Root fragments lay scattered, the lighter wood of recent breaks exposed to air. The ground around the tree's base was disturbed in a pattern that made no sense at first—the soil was gouged and displaced as though something very heavy and very slow had rolled there, pressing and releasing, pressing and releasing in a rhythm like breathing.

Luca's chest tightened. He was fourteen now, old enough to work without close watching, old enough to notice when the world behaved in ways his elders had not prepared him for. He sat back on his heels and looked at the tree again.

The roots. The massive roots that had held the trunk upright against the wind had moved. The displacement pattern showed it clearly once he understood what he was seeing. The tree had not fallen. It had not broken. It had simply... shifted. Relocated. The roots had lifted from the earth, found new purchase perhaps three full paces from where they had been, and settled into the ground as though they had been waiting for this place all along.

He stood and walked slowly around the tree, noting the details with the meticulous attention that had kept him from losing sheep in the mountain passes. The resin on the northern side of the trunk was darker, as though it had wept recently and then dried to a harder consistency. The bark showed no damage. The needles responded to the wind with their normal slight tremor. Everything was intact.

Everything was alive.

What he had found was not a catastrophe but evidence of something for which he had no name.

He stayed through the afternoon, until the light began its collapse toward the ridge. He did not tell anyone. Instead, he returned the sheep to the lower pastures with excuses about needing to scout new forage higher up, then made his way back to the tree alone in the first darkness.

This became the shape of his autumn. During the day he moved the flocks and performed the tasks his family expected of him. At night, and whenever he could extract himself from observation, he climbed toward the heights. He began carrying a stick, a shepherd's staff carved and worn smooth by his grandfather, and he used it to mark the ground around the tree. Not obviously—small nicks against the limestone, pressure marks in the soil. If the tree moved again, he would know by how much and in what direction.

His mother noticed his absence. His father asked where he was going so often. His younger sister Elia followed him once and then stopped following when he was unkind about it, told her she was too slow, that the heights were dangerous, that he was old enough to be trusted but she was not. She was only eight and accepted this reasoning because it was the tone of someone who knew the mountains.

He did return to the tree. A week after his first discovery, the marks had shifted. The displacement pattern had advanced perhaps the width of a hand toward the southwest, and new resin had bled from the cambium in a line that seemed to follow the tree's rotation. He added new marks and returned three days later to find them moved again.

The tree was walking.

This knowledge settled into his chest like a stone. He did not speak it aloud. He did not write it. He simply carried it with him, this impossible fact, and arranged his life around protecting it.

By mid-winter, the pattern was clear enough that he could anticipate the next movement within a day or two. The tree moved slowly—a pace or less with each shift—and only after certain conditions were met. Heavy rain appeared to trigger movement. A particular wind direction that came down the limestone faces seemed to encourage it. But there were other variables, factors he could not parse, and this uncertainty became something he cultivated rather than resisted.

He was the only one who knew.

The thought was large enough to contain him entirely some days.

It was in the snow that fell in February that he first truly understood how singular his knowledge was. Snow collected on the displacement sites and marked them clearly for anyone who looked. But no one came this far into the heights anymore. The pilgrimage routes had shifted a generation ago, and the shepherds from the lower villages kept to safer terrain. He was alone with the tree, and the tree was moving under his sole attention, answering in its slow way to pressures and seasons and patterns that seemed written in the ground itself.

He was fashioning a new set of marks, using stones this time instead of scratches, when a voice reached him from the tree line.

"You're not praying, I think."

Luca's hands froze. He did not turn around. The voice was male, measured, carrying an accent that suggested the mountain villages higher up, or perhaps somewhere beyond them. When Luca finally turned, he found a man standing perhaps twenty paces away, half-shadowed by the pines. The man was perhaps forty, or perhaps sixty—there was something in his build that made age difficult to read. His hair was dark, threaded with gray at the temples. His hands were visible at his sides, empty and still.

"You climb here alone," the man continued. It was not a question. "Multiple times. Your marks are visible if you know how to read the ground. You're careful, but not careful enough." The man's eyes moved to the tree. "What are you looking for?"

"Shelter," Luca said, the lie emerging fast. "In case the weather turns."

"There's better shelter lower down. The ruins near the spring. You'd be out of the wind, at least." The man was still looking at the tree. "You're not a shepherd keeping lost animals from straying. I've watched how you move. You're counting something."

Luca's throat felt narrow. He could run—he knew the terrain better than this stranger did—but something in the man's stance suggested that running would be answered with pursuit, and he was already breathing hard from the work of climbing. Instead, he said nothing and waited.

"Your excuses are poor," the man said finally. "Every time someone asks why you're going into the heights, your answer changes. First it's prayer. Then it's a lost ewe. Then it's checking traps. A different lie each time means you're trying to hide something, not protect a habit." The man turned to face him directly. "What's worth lying so badly about?"

The storm came that night, moving in from the west with the speed of something alive and hunting. Luca had been heading down the slope, moving quickly because the light was failing and because the stranger had unsettled him in ways he couldn't name. The wind came first, then the rain turning to sleet, then the darkness compressing everything into a narrow space where up was just a direction of greater cold.

He sheltered in a rock outcropping he knew, the one the man had mentioned—the ruins near the spring, though he'd never thought of them as ruins before. They were just old stone, fitted without mortar in a way that suggested someone had built them a very long time ago for a purpose that was no longer remembered. The shelter was deep enough that he could fit inside it, and the mouth was narrow enough to deflect most of the wind. He waited there through the night, listening to the storm shatter itself against the rock, thinking about the stranger and his careful questions and his knowledge of marks that should have been invisible.

When the morning came, it came wrong. The air was still. The rain had stopped. But the wind had changed direction, and with it had come something else—a smell of burnt stone, of ozone, of air that had been split open and was still bleeding the memory of its splitting. Luca stepped out of the shelter and climbed toward the ridge.

The tree was wrong.

Not fallen. Not broken. But its position had shifted violently. The displacement pattern was no longer a slow, measured series of movements. It was a single massive displacement, as though the tree had been seized and twisted by something with terrible strength. The roots on the eastern side had been torn, exposing the pale wood underneath. The resin was darker than he'd ever seen it, nearly black in places, and it had bled down the trunk in thick rivulets that had hardened to a glassy state.

But what caught his attention was the scorched earth.

A line of burnt stone ran from a point perhaps fifty paces away directly to the tree's exposed roots. The limestone was blackened, cracked from the heat, and in places the surface had fractured completely, leaving gaps where ash had settled. The grass was gone. The smaller plants had been carbonized to nothing.

Lightning, Luca understood. A direct strike. So close to the tree that the energy had burned the ground black.

He climbed closer, his hands shaking. The tree's bark was intact on most of the trunk, but on the south-facing side there was a mark—a long, shallow scar that ran from the height of his head down toward the roots. The scar was still oozing resin, fresh and warm to the touch.

The tree had survived.

He should have been afraid. Instead, he knelt again and placed his hand on the warm bark, feeling the pulse of the resin, the steady presence of growth continuing beneath the damage. The tree was still alive. The tree was still moving.

The knowledge settled deeper now, past the stone in his chest, into something more fundamental.

He heard the footsteps before he saw the figure emerging from the smoke-hazed air. The same man from yesterday, moving slowly, deliberately. His hands were visible again, empty again. But there was something about him that had changed. His right hand was burned, the palm dark red and blistering. His left hand was worse—the skin had split in places, and the underlying tissue was raw and wept serum that had darkened to a crust.

"So you're the only one watching," the man said. He was breathing heavily, as though he'd run far and fast. "That's good. That's necessary. If others knew..." He trailed off, looking at Luca with eyes that seemed much older than the face containing them. "You need to be more careful. And you need to understand that what you're protecting is worth protecting."

"What's your name?" Luca asked.

"Farovald," the man said. "I was here when the storm happened. Before you were born, before your father was born. I was... nearby." He looked at his burned hands as though they belonged to someone else. "The lightning found us both. It changed us. But you're not seeing that, and you need to stay unseen for the rest of your life. Your family thinks you're odd already. Your mother mentioned it—that you wander, that you're distant, that you love the cold and the dark more than other children. Let them think that. Let them think you're praying when you come here. Prayer is something that makes sense to them. Prayer is safe."

"Did the lightning..." Luca couldn't finish the sentence. The question was too large, and he didn't have the words to contain it.

"Change me?" Farovald flexed his burned hands carefully, wincing. "Yes. But not the way you're thinking. I'm not magic. The tree isn't magic. What happened was real, which is harder than magic. It was three things at once—the lightning, the stone, the fungal networks running through the limestone like veins. They all met at the same moment, and the meeting changed the shape of what we are." He looked at the tree again. "It doesn't speak. It doesn't think the way you do. But it feels things. It knows pressure, and chemistry, and the slow patience of roots. And now it can move."

"Why?" Luca asked.

"Because it was struck while it was growing. The lightning restructured the cellular architecture. The roots aren't tendons—they're more than that now. They can articulate in ways pine roots shouldn't be able to. The tree is learning how to use them."

Farovald sat down heavily on the blackened stone. "You're going to be its guardian. I can see that already, the way you're attending to it. It will take you decades to understand what that means. The tree will probably outlive you by centuries. It will move, and you'll learn to move with it. You'll protect the knowledge of it, carry it forward, pass it to someone else when you're too old to maintain the care yourself. And the tree will do what trees do—grow, and endure, and continue."

"Why can't you do it?" Luca asked. "You were here first."

"Because I can't be what it needs. I'm temporary by comparison. I was struck in the event, yes, and I survived, and I've changed in ways that let me sense what it's doing. But I wasn't rooted. I'm still human. I still move through the world in human ways. The tree needs someone anchored in time and place. Someone who can learn the patterns." Farovald stood again, with effort. "Someone young enough to develop the habit of attention."

He turned to leave, then stopped. "Your sister. She followed you once. Don't let her come back here again. Not yet. Not until you're ready to teach her."

"How long will that be?" Luca asked.

"Years," Farovald said. "Maybe decades. Long enough that she'll have her own life, her own concerns, and you'll have to convince her that she wants this responsibility. That's the hardest part of guardianship—not the care itself, but the passing of it forward to someone who has to choose to carry it."

He moved back toward the tree line, then paused one final time. "Prayer," he said. "Use it. Tell your family you come here to pray. It's close enough to the truth that it won't feel like a lie to them, and it gives you the cover you need. The mountains are full of holy men and women seeking solitude. They'll understand prayer. They won't understand what you're actually doing."

Then he was gone, moving back into the pines with a careful, measured step that suggested his burned hands were not the only thing the lightning had damaged.

Luca remained with the tree through the morning, reading the displacement pattern, understanding that something fundamental had shifted in the night. The movement was no longer predictable. The tree had reacted to the strike with a massive repositioning, and he would have to recalibrate his observations, his marks, his understanding of what the tree needed.

He descended as the day climbed toward its zenith, telling his mother that he'd been praying in the heights, that the thunder had frightened him but he was safe. She believed him because he looked frightened, and he was—though not of the thunder. She served him bread and cheese without comment, understanding only that her strange boy had sought comfort in the old ways, and that was good. That was normal, even if nothing else about him was.

That night, as he lay in the darkness of the stone house, listening to the wind in the eaves, Luca understood what Farovald had meant about guardianship. It wasn't a burden that could be carried lightly. It was the kind of knowledge that changed the shape of everything—your family, your work, your place in the village. It was a secret that would require him to construct a life around protecting it, to become someone who could move through the world with patience and attention, noticing patterns that others would never see, marking time in a way that served something older and stranger than himself.

The tree would continue to move. He would continue to return. His life had already begun its long reorientation toward a task he'd never known existed three days before.

But that knowledge was his alone now. His to carry, his to develop, his to eventually pass forward to someone else—someone who would stand in the same place he stood now, kneeling in the cold, learning to read the language of displaced earth and living wood and the endless patience of a tree that had learned, against all probability, how to walk.
